No slides were given for this lecture. The notes of Alessa, Alsalamah and Alomar word for word, in their own order (green), every gift (red) under the part it belongs to.

Notes

General Approach to Lower GI Bleeding

Every patient with GI bleeding gets the same systematic sequence. The differential drives the investigations — not the other way round.

StepWhat it involves
HistoryCharacter of bleeding, pain vs painless, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, prior episodes, screening history.
ExaminationFull abdominal assessment.
DREDigital rectal examination is part of the examination, not an optional add-on. Always assess for local/perianal causes.
Labs + adjunctsLabs, imaging, endoscopy — selected according to the differential.
ImpressionEstablish a differential → commit to a top differential → order targeted investigations.
RULE OF THUMB
Investigations must be judicious and tailored to what you are ruling in or out. Do not order unnecessary tests.
CONTEXT
The small bowel accounts for only about 5% of GI bleeding cases — which is why it is a diagnosis of exclusion after upper and colonic sources are addressed.
Notes

Diverticular Disease — One Lesion, Two Diseases

A diverticulum is a mucosal/submucosal outpouching herniating through a weak point in the colonic wall — specifically where the vessels penetrate. That anatomy explains both of its complications.

DIVERTICULUM
Thin-walled outpouching at the point of vessel penetration through the colonic wall
Vessel ruptures DIVERTICULAR BLEEDING More often the RIGHT colon Painless, sudden, can be massive Often self-limited, may re-bleed ~1/3 of all acute LGIB Surgery = subtotal colectomy·Inflammation / perforation DIVERTICULITIS Usually SIGMOID / left colon LLQ pain, fever, malaise ~75% of episodes uncomplicated NOT a typical cause of LGIB Surgery = segmental sigmoidectomy
★ HIGH-YIELD DISTINCTION
Diverticular bleeding is not diverticulitis. They arise from the same diverticula but are usually separate clinical entities — different colonic side, different presentation, different operation. Diverticulitis is not a typical cause of lower GI bleeding.
  • Landmark separating upper from lower GI bleeding → duodenojejunal junction (ligament of Treitz). 434 ×2
Diverticular bleeding is NOT diverticulitis — same diverticula, different side, presentation and operation.
Notes

Diverticulosis — the background

By age 60, roughly 50% of people have diverticulosis.
Only a small proportion ever become symptomatic.
Associated with constipation and a low-fibre diet; increasingly common locally.
Right-sided diverticulitis is relatively more common in Asian populations.
Notes

Diverticular Bleeding

Clinical features

The most common cause of acute lower GI bleeding — approximately one-third of LGIB cases.
Characteristically painless, sudden, and potentially massive/brisk hematochezia.
Often self-limited — it bleeds, stops, and may bleed again.
Always ask specifically about anticoagulants and NSAID use.
RECURRENCE
Short-term recurrent bleeding occurs in around 50%. Lifetime recurrence is approximately 15–25% in patients managed without resection.
  • Massive painless haematochezia, diverticula everywhere but none bleeding at colonoscopy → source → vasa recta. 442
Notes

Initial management of significant acute LGIB

For the actively or profusely bleeding patient, resuscitate first, investigate second:

Assess hemodynamic stability and vitals
IV access
IV fluids
Check Hb
NPO
Blood transfusion when indicated

Only then investigate and localise the bleeding source.

TAILOR TO THE PATIENT
A stable chronic or clinic patient does not automatically need emergency IV resuscitation. The approach is tailored to the clinical condition in front of you.
Notes

Localising & Treating Diverticular Bleeding

The four modalities differ mainly in how slow a bleed they can detect and whether they can treat it. Learn the thresholds — they are classic exam material.

ModalityDetectsRole & key pointsCan treat?
1. Colonoscopy—Usually the initial investigation after stabilisation. Identifies the source and excludes other causes (malignancy, anorectal source). Bleeding has often stopped by the time you scope, so the exact diverticulum may not be identifiable.Yes — epinephrine injection, thermal/coagulation, other local techniques
2. CT angiography≈ 0.3 mL/minUsed when colonoscopy shows blood but cannot localise the source. Non-invasive and highly accurate for localisation.No
3. Catheter angiography≈ 0.5 mL/minInvasive vascular cannulation — the least sensitive threshold, but its major advantage is therapeutic.Yes — immediate angiographic embolization
4. Tagged RBC scan≈ 0.1 mL/minNuclear medicine study. Most sensitive for very slow bleeding, but poor localisation — approximately 25% false localisation.No
★ WHY THE TESTS COME BACK NEGATIVE
All localisation tests work best during active bleeding. Because diverticular haemorrhage is often intermittent and self-limited, the study may be entirely negative once the bleeding stops.
DANGER
Never empirically embolize an unlocalised vessel — you risk bowel ischemia. The principle is always localise → then treat/embolize.
All localisation tests need active bleeding. Never embolize an unlocalised vessel (bowel ischaemia) — localise first, then treat.
  • Most useful imaging to localise active lower GI bleeding → CT angiography (stable/inactive → colonoscopy). 435 ×5
Notes

Surgery for Uncontrolled Diverticular Bleeding

When to operate

The bleeding source cannot be controlled or localised.
Persistent major bleeding despite resuscitation and transfusion.
Approximately 4–6 units PRBC required within 24 hours.
Bleeding continues for approximately 72 hours.
  • Same woman collapses, SBP 80 despite transfusion → transfusion + laparotomy + total colectomy. 426
Notes

The operation

ElementDetail
ProcedureTotal abdominal (subtotal) colectomy — the entire colon is removed, the rectum is preserved.
ReconstructionDepends on patient and intraoperative condition: ileorectal anastomosis or ileostomy.
Why keep the rectum?The rectum does not typically develop diverticulosis, because the taeniae coli converge there. It is therefore generally not the bleeding source.
MortalityThe emergency operation carries approximately 25% mortality.
LECTURE EMPHASIS
Avoid a limited/segmental colectomy for uncontrolled, unidentified diverticular haemorrhage — because of the risk of recurrent bleeding from the colon you left behind. Some algorithms do permit segmental resection when the site is clearly localised.
Operation: total abdominal (subtotal) colectomy, rectum preserved (ileorectal anastomosis or ileostomy) — ~25% mortality. Avoid a segmental resection for unlocalised bleeding (re-bleeding from the colon left behind). The rectum is spared because the taeniae coli converge there (no diverticula).
Notes

Follow-up after diverticular bleeding

No routine serial colonoscopy simply because diverticulosis was found.
Counsel the patient that bleeding can recur and to return to the ER if it does.
Later colonoscopy should be for another indication — e.g. colorectal cancer screening or polyp surveillance.
Screening is discussed from age 45. A normal screening colonoscopy → usual interval approximately 10 years; the interval changes according to polyp/dysplasia findings.
Notes

Diverticulitis

Uncomplicated vs complicated

The definition is simply the presence or absence of four complications. About 75% of episodes are uncomplicated.

UncomplicatedComplicated — any one of:
Inflammation without abscess, perforation, fistula, or stricture/obstruction.Abscess · Perforation · Fistula · Stricture / obstruction
Presentation and diagnosis
DomainFindings
Typical presentationLeft lower quadrant pain (the sigmoid is the commonest site), fever, malaise/systemic symptoms. Right-sided pain is possible with right-sided disease — relatively more common in Asian populations.
LabsLeukocytosis, ↑ CRP, ↑ ESR.
Definitive testCT abdomen — establishes the diagnosis and evaluates complications.
But firstHistory and examination still come first, and DRE is part of the examination.
Hinchey classification
★ MUST KNOW
Hinchey classifies complicated diverticulitis and it changes management — the I–II / III–IV split is the operative dividing line.
StageFindingImplication
Hinchey 0No major complication / uncomplicated disease
Hinchey ISmall / localised pericolic abscessOften managed non-operatively if the patient is stable.
Hinchey IILarger, distant or pelvic abscess
Hinchey IIIPurulent peritonitisOften confirmed intraoperatively and
Hinchey IVFecal peritonitisgenerally requires surgery.
Management of complicated diverticulitis
ScenarioManagement
Abscess < 3 cm (stable patient)Usually too small for percutaneous drainage → IV antibiotics and supportive treatment.
Abscess > 3 cm (stable patient)IR-guided percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics.
Supportive care for bothIV access · hydration · bowel rest · admission.
Straight to ORHemodynamic instability · peritonitis / acute abdomen · free perforation · Hinchey III–IV.
★ WHICH COMPLICATION CAN BE TALKED OUT OF SURGERY?
Among the complications, an abscess is the main one that may resolve with conservative/IR management. Fistula, stricture/obstruction, and major perforation will generally not resolve definitively with conservative treatment and usually require surgery.
The abscess is the one complication that can be talked out of surgery. Fistula, stricture/obstruction and major perforation usually need surgery.
Notes

Colonoscopy after diverticulitis

A CT showing diverticulitis does not completely exclude an underlying colorectal cancer.
Approximate occult malignancy risk: complicated diverticulitis ≈ 11% vs uncomplicated ≈ 1% — so colonoscopy matters most after complicated disease.
Do not scope during acute inflammation — increased perforation risk. Wait until the acute episode resolves.
Anyone ≥ 45 years who has not had appropriate screening should undergo screening colonoscopy regardless.
CLASSIC EXAM TEACHING
Colonoscopy after an episode of diverticulitis, once inflammation resolves. The rationale is to exclude hidden malignancy, especially after complicated disease.
Notes

Surgery for diverticulitis

SettingOperation and principle
EmergencyPerforation, peritonitis, or acute abdomen → emergency surgery.
ElectiveUsually segmental resection — most commonly sigmoidectomy. Unlike uncontrolled haemorrhage, do not remove the whole colon just because diverticula exist elsewhere. Remove the segment responsible for the recurrent inflammatory disease.
★ CURRENT INDICATION PRINCIPLE
The decision is individualised according to quality of life — not simply patient age or a fixed number of attacks.
3 attacks spread over many years → may have little QoL impact.
3 attacks within one year with repeated hospitalisation and work interruption → may justify surgery. Elective surgery may also be considered after complicated diverticulitis. Fistula, stricture, and obstruction are stronger indications because they are unlikely to disappear with conservative treatment.
Notes

Angiodysplasia

A dilated submucosal vascular lesion with a feeding vessel, commonly found in the right colon of elderly patients.

FeatureDetail
PrevalenceFound incidentally in approximately 2% of asymptomatic patients undergoing colonoscopy.
Clinical impactOnly about 15% develop clinically significant bleeding → ~85% remain asymptomatic.
Bleeding patternUsually slow and intermittent, unlike brisk diverticular haemorrhage. May present as chronic occult blood loss / iron-deficiency anemia.
TreatmentEndoscopic therapy is usually successful: injection therapy, thermal/electrocoagulation/bipolar therapy, endoscopic clips when appropriate.
SurgeryRarely required.
LEAVE IT ALONE
Incidentally detected, asymptomatic angiodysplasia generally does not require intervention.
  • Haematochezia with 3rd-degree haemorrhoids in a 62-year-old → colonoscopy first (> 45) 436 ×2; 20-year-old with haemorrhoids but family history of colon cancer and iron-deficiency anaemia → colonoscopy. 439 ×2
Notes

Colitis as a Cause of LGIB

Colitis = inflammation of the colonic wall. It usually causes smaller-volume bleeding rather than massive haemorrhage — though ulcerative colitis may produce significant bloody diarrhoea.

Inflammatory bowel disease
Ulcerative colitis
Ischemic colitis
Radiation colitis
Infectious colitis
  • Elderly diabetic, LLQ pain, bloody diarrhoea, fever, leukocytosis, thumb-printing of descending/sigmoid colon → ischaemic colitis 434 ×3; thumbprint sign → ischaemic colitis. 434
  • Recurrent fistula, bloody mucus, tenesmus, unhealthy rectum → keyed Crohn's or UC (fistula favours Crohn's; rectal involvement and bloody mucus favour UC). 427
  • Young woman with IBD (mild colitis a year ago), now haematochezia → Crohn's flare (or CRC — colitis raises cancer risk). 441
Notes

Ischemic colitis

Caused by inadequate blood flow to a segment of colon.

Embolic/mechanical vascular occlusion can occur, but more commonly it arises in elderly, sick, or dehydrated patients in a low-flow/hypotensive state.
Affects vulnerable watershed areas — classically the splenic flexure.
Management: correct the cause. For low-flow ischemia → IV hydration, NPO, antibiotics/supportive care. Often self-limiting once perfusion is restored.
If a true mechanical vascular obstruction is present, the mechanical cause must be treated.
★ DO NOT CONFUSE THESE TWO
Ischemic colitis and mesenteric ischemia are different organs, different mechanisms, and different levels of urgency.
Ischemic colitisMesenteric ischemia
OrganColonPrimarily small bowel
MechanismCommonly non-occlusive / low-flowCommonly mechanical arterial occlusion / embolism
TerritoryOften watershed (splenic flexure)Arterial distribution — classic example: atrial fibrillation → arterial embolus → small- bowel ischemia/infarction
UrgencyFrequently improves with conservative/supportive treatmentA true emergency
Infectious colitis
• Presents with bloody diarrhoea due to inflamed colonic mucosa.
• Diarrhoea occurs because the inflamed colon cannot normally absorb water.
• Investigate with stool culture when infection is suspected.
• Organisms mentioned: E. coli, Campylobacter, Shigella.
Treat the underlying infection → the colitis and bleeding usually resolve.
  • Elderly man, bleeding with diarrhoea, LIF pain, thick sigmoid on X-ray → fluids and antibiotics. 428
  • 10–15 episodes of bloody diarrhoea, dehydrated, hypotensive, cachectic → admit and rehydrate with IV fluids 437 436 ×2
  • Fever, 6 bloody stools, leukocytosis, generalized tenderness → keyed colectomy. 427
Notes

Massive Hematochezia — Do Not Miss an Upper GI Source

★ THE TRAP
In massive hematochezia with hemodynamic compromise, always consider a brisk upper GI bleed presenting per rectum.

Evaluation still begins the same way: history → physical examination → DRE, checking for hemorrhoidal/anorectal sources, with endoscopic evaluation as indicated.

StepAction
Assess upper sourceUpper endoscopy, or NG tube assessment as discussed.
If no upper sourceColonoscopy.
Still not foundCTA / tagged RBC scan / catheter angiography as needed.
PrincipleFind the source → treat it. If not found, continue down the localisation algorithm.
Blood appearance and localisation
AppearanceSuggests
Bright red bloodGenerally a fresh / distal source — hemorrhoids, rectal or distal colonic lesions.
Darker, mixed with stoolMore proximal bleeding spends longer in the bowel, so it mixes with stool and darkens.
MelenaThink more proximal — particularly upper GI or small bowel.
Fresh or clottedLeft-sided colonic bleeding may appear as either fresh or clotted blood.
ASK THESE FOUR QUESTIONS
Fresh or dark? · Liquid or clotted? · Melena? · Mixed with stool?
INDICATOR, NOT A RULE
Blood colour is an indicator, not an absolute rule. Hemorrhoidal blood can clot if retained temporarily in the rectum — so clots do not automatically mean a proximal lesion. The purpose is to estimate distal vs proximal; definitive localisation requires investigation.
Massive haematochezia with haemodynamic compromise → always consider a brisk upper GI bleed. History → exam → DRE → upper endoscopy (or NG assessment) → no upper source → colonoscopy → still not found → CTA / tagged RBC scan / catheter angiography.
  • Bleeding per rectum with a normal colonoscopy → next upper GI endoscopy to exclude an upper source. 426
  • 70-year-old, massive fresh PR bleeding without pain, shocked, NG drains green fluid → keyed angiodysplasia 434 ×2; massive PR bleeding, Hb 6, shocked → angiodysplasia. 429
  • 70-year-old: bright red blood mixed with stool, constipation, weight loss, pale → colon cancer. 436 ×6

Diverticular bleeding ≠ diverticulitis. Bleeding is painless, sudden, often massive, more often right colon. Diverticulitis is LLQ pain + fever, sigmoid/left colon — and is not a typical cause of LGIB. Diverticular bleeding is the most common cause of acute LGIB (~1/3 of cases), is often self-limited, recurs short-term in ~50%, and has a 15–25% lifetime recurrence without resection.

Detection thresholds: tagged RBC scan 0.1 mL/min (most sensitive, ~25% false localisation) < CT angiography 0.3 mL/min (non-invasive, accurate) < catheter angiography 0.5 mL/min (invasive, but can embolize). All localisation tests need active bleeding — and never embolize an unlocalised vessel (bowel ischemia). Localise first, then treat.

Two different operations. Uncontrolled/unlocalised diverticular haemorrhage → subtotal (total abdominal) colectomy, rectum preserved (~25% mortality). Diverticulitis → segmental sigmoidectomy. The rectum is spared in diverticular disease because the taeniae coli converge there — which is why it is preserved at subtotal colectomy.

Surgical triggers for bleeding: 4–6 units PRBC in 24 h, bleeding for ~72 h, or an uncontrollable/unlocalisable source.

Hinchey I–II (localised then distant/pelvic abscess) can often be managed non-operatively; Hinchey III (purulent) and IV (fecal peritonitis) generally require surgery.

Abscess is the one complication that may resolve conservatively — <3 cm antibiotics alone, >3 cm IR drainage + antibiotics. Fistula, stricture/obstruction, and major perforation usually need surgery. Scope after diverticulitis, never during it (perforation risk). Occult malignancy risk is ~11% after complicated vs ~1% after uncomplicated disease. Screening applies from age 45.

Elective surgery for diverticulitis is decided by quality-of-life impact, not age or a fixed attack count.

Angiodysplasia: right colon, elderly, 2% incidental, only 15% bleed significantly. Bleeding is slow/intermittent → iron-deficiency anemia. Endoscopic therapy usually works; surgery rarely needed.

Ischemic colitis = colon, low-flow, watershed (splenic flexure), often conservative. Mesenteric ischemia = small bowel, embolic (classically AF), a true emergency.

In massive hematochezia with instability, rule out a brisk upper GI bleed before chasing the colon.

Blood colour guides but does not prove: bright red suggests distal, melena suggests proximal — but hemorrhoidal blood can clot in the rectum, so clots do not mean a proximal lesion.

  • Elderly woman, painless rectal bleeding, stable, similar attacks before → diverticulosis 426; painless massive rectal bleeding, NG aspirate bile without blood → diverticulosis. 431
  • Angiodysplasia with massive bleeding, unstable → angiographic embolization (surgery if it fails). 427 429 ×3
  • Painful bright red bleeding, worst during and after defecation → anal fissure 430 ×2 429 ×2
